outline: Diffraction is the spreading of waves when they pass through an aperture or around an edge. In a ripple tank, plane water waves reach a barrier with a gap and spread into curved wavefronts beyond it. The amount of spreading depends on the wavelength relative to the gap width: it is pronounced when they are comparable and smaller when the gap is much wider. At unchanged depth, passing through a gap does not change wave speed, frequency or wavelength. Use $v=f\lambda$ when a frequency change is given.

misconceptions.refutation: Diffraction is spreading at a gap or edge; neither a change of medium nor bouncing back is required.
misconceptions.contrast: A wave spreads into the geometrical shadow beyond an aperture or edge.

misconceptions.statement: A wider gap gives more spreading.
misconceptions.refutation: For fixed wavelength, a wider gap gives less diffraction.
misconceptions.contrast: Spreading is most marked when gap width is comparable to wavelength.

misconceptions.statement: Passing through a gap changes wavelength.
misconceptions.refutation: The medium and frequency remain the same, so wave speed and wavelength remain the same.
misconceptions.contrast: Gap width changes the spread, not wavefront spacing.

misconceptions.statement: Increasing amplitude increases the diffraction angle.
misconceptions.refutation: Diffraction depends on wavelength relative to gap width, not amplitude.
misconceptions.contrast: Greater amplitude makes waves larger, not more spread out.

items.stem: A sound wave of wavelength 0.50 m passes through a doorway of width 1.0 m between two rooms. Which change increases the amount of diffraction that takes place?

options.A: Double the amplitude of the sound wave.
options.B: Double the width of the doorway.
options.C: Halve the frequency of the sound wave.
options.D: Halve the period of the sound wave.

items.explanation: Halving frequency doubles wavelength to 1.0 m, matching the doorway. Increasing amplitude changes size, not spread; widening the doorway reduces diffraction.

items.stem: Water waves of wavelength λ are incident normally on an obstacle with a narrow gap. The width of the gap is equal to λ. The waves from the gap emerge over an angle θ as shown. The gap is slowly widened. Which changes, if any, occur to θ and to the wavelength of the emerging waves?
items.explanation: As the gap widens relative to wavelength, θ decreases. The same medium means the wavelength stays unchanged; B reverses the angular trend.

items.stem: Water waves of wavelength λ are incident normally on an obstacle with a narrow gap. The width of the gap is equal to λ. The waves from the gap emerge over an angle θ, as shown. The gap is slowly widened. Which changes, if any, occur to θ and to the wavelength of the emerging waves?
items.explanation: A wider gap produces less spreading, so θ decreases without changing wavelength. B was popular but assumes wider gaps cause more diffraction.

items.stem: A light wave passes through a single slit and a diffraction pattern forms. What happens to the frequency and the speed of the wave when it is diffracted?
items.explanation: Diffraction in the same medium changes direction distribution, not frequency or speed. C incorrectly assumes speed decreases.

items.stem: An electromagnetic wave is diffracted as it passes through a single slit. The width of the slit is larger than the wavelength of the wave. Which change will decrease the amount of diffraction of the wave?

options.A: Decrease the frequency of the wave.
options.B: Decrease the time period of the wave.
options.C: Decrease the width of the slit.
options.D: Increase the wavelength of the wave.

items.explanation: Decreasing period increases frequency, reducing wavelength at fixed speed and therefore reducing diffraction. C makes the slit narrower and increases spreading.

items.stem: A teacher is explaining diffraction to a group of students. Which piece of apparatus is most appropriate for the teacher to use to demonstrate diffraction?
items.explanation: A ripple tank clearly shows plane wavefronts spreading after a gap. A spring does not show two-dimensional spreading as clearly.

items.stem: In which situation does diffraction occur?

options.A: A wave bounces back from a surface.
options.B: A wave passes from one medium into another.
options.C: A wave passes through a gap in a barrier.
options.D: Waves from two identical sources are superposed.

items.explanation: Passing through a gap can make a wave spread. A describes reflection, a different behaviour.

items.stem: A water wave in a ripple tank is diffracted as it passes through a gap in a barrier. Which two factors affect the angle of diffraction of the wave?

options.A: the amplitude and frequency of the incident wave
options.B: the amplitude of the incident wave and the width of the gap
options.C: the wavelength and amplitude of the incident wave
options.D: the wavelength of the incident wave and the width of the gap

items.explanation: The ratio of wavelength to gap width controls spreading. Amplitude changes wave height, not the angle.

items.stem: What is meant by diffraction?

options.A: the change in observed frequency when a wave source moves relative to an observer
options.B: the formation of nodes and antinodes by two progressive waves travelling in opposite directions
options.C: the spreading of a wave around the edge of an obstacle
options.D: the superposition of two waves when they meet

items.explanation: Diffraction is spreading around an edge. D describes superposition and does not require an edge.

items.stem: Which waves would best demonstrate diffraction through a doorway?
items.explanation: Sound wavelengths can be comparable with doorway width, so they spread appreciably. Visible-light wavelength is far smaller.

items.stem: A water wave passes through a gap in a harbour wall and diffracts. The gap has a width of 8 m. The wave travels directly towards the gap. For which wavelength is the diffraction of the wave greatest?
items.explanation: A wavelength equal to the 8 m gap gives the greatest spreading among these options. The 1 m wave is much shorter and spreads less.

items.stem: An experiment is set up to demonstrate the diffraction of water waves in a ripple tank. The waves pass through a gap of width w and some diffraction of the waves is observed. The wavelength of the waves is now doubled. What is the new gap width needed to cause the same amount of diffraction as before?
items.explanation: The wavelength-to-width ratio must stay constant, so doubling wavelength requires doubling gap width. B leaves the gap unchanged and increases spreading.

flashcards.back: The spreading of waves as they pass through an aperture or around the edge of an obstacle.

9702-8.2.1.motivate: Why can you hear someone speaking around a corner even when you cannot see them? A wave can spread into a region beyond an opening or edge.
9702-8.2.1.establish: Diffraction means the spreading of waves as they pass through an aperture or around the edge of an obstacle. Plane waves reaching a narrow gap emerge as curved wavefronts that spread into the shadow region. Diffraction is a wave phenomenon and occurs for water waves, sound and light. The wave does not need a new medium: it can spread while its speed, frequency and wavelength remain unchanged.
9702-8.2.1.connect: This builds on wavelength and wavefronts. The spacing between consecutive crests can stay the same even while the wavefronts change direction and curve around an edge.
9702-8.2.1.note:
- Diffraction: spreading of waves through a gap or around an edge.
- Wavefronts curve into the region beyond the barrier.
- It is a wave behaviour, not a change of medium.
9702-8.2.1.self_explain: What two parts must a complete definition of diffraction include?

options.A: A wave reflects from a wall.
options.B: A wave spreads beyond the edge of a barrier.
options.C: A wave slows in a new medium.

discover.explanation: Spreading around an obstacle edge is diffraction.

9702-8.2.2.motivate: A ripple tank lets you see how the same waves behave at wide and narrow gaps. The visible change is the angle through which the wavefronts spread.
9702-8.2.2.establish: Use a vibrating straight bar to produce plane water waves in a ripple tank. Place a barrier with a gap across their path and observe the waves before and after it. The emerging wavefronts curve and spread: this demonstrates diffraction. Compare gap width $w$ with wavelength $\lambda$ (the spacing of adjacent crests). Spreading is pronounced when $w$ is comparable with $\lambda$; when $w$ is much wider, the spread is smaller. At fixed water depth, speed is approximately constant. The vibrator fixes frequency, so passing through the gap leaves speed, frequency and wavelength unchanged. To increase spreading, narrow the gap or, at constant depth, lower the frequency: $v=f\lambda$ then gives a larger wavelength.
9702-8.2.2.connect: Use $v=f\lambda$ from progressive waves to reason about changing frequency. The key comparison is wavelength relative to gap width, not amplitude.
9702-8.2.2.note:
- Make plane waves with a straight vibrator; direct them through a gap.
- Wavefronts spread more when gap width is comparable with wavelength.
- Widening the gap reduces the spread at fixed wavelength.
- At unchanged depth, the gap does not change wavelength.
9702-8.2.2.self_explain: If the gap widens at fixed water depth and vibrator frequency, what happens to the spread and wavelength?

discover.stem: A gap is much wider than the water-wave wavelength. Which change makes spreading more obvious?

options.D: Increase water depth without any other information.

discover.explanation: Narrowing the gap makes its width closer to the wavelength, so the wave spreads more.
